segments.title: The scenario and the alerts
sections: Six Hours Of Watching, Nothing To Show
Alerts At Levels, Not Eyes On Every Candle

cues.text: The plan was done by 9:25 a.m. The levels were marked. Then you watched every one-minute candle for six and a half hours.
By 1:40 p.m. you took a trade from the middle of the range, because something had to happen.
At 4:05 p.m. the platform was still open, and the journal said only what the account said.
Nothing in that day was a market problem. The session had no shape you had chosen, and the day had no end.
This module gives it both. Six parts, mechanical first: alerts.
Your plan marks each level as a zone, a band with two edges. The near edge is the one price reaches first. The far edge is the one behind it.
Your stop, the resting order that takes you out if the level fails, goes behind the far edge.
A level alert is a sound-on alert you set on a zone before the session. Every zone carries two.
One: an alert at the near edge. It calls you to the screen, because the level test is happening now, and the trigger, the price event that puts you in, can only fire from here.
Two: an alert at the far edge. Price has traded through the whole zone. If you are in a trade from that level, your stop is the next thing price meets.
Between alerts, the chart does not need you. Price sixty points from a zone is not a trade. It is weather.
In NinjaTrader 8, click the line or rectangle you drew at the level.
Choose Alert, and set the action to play a sound.
Rearm decides whether an alert can fire again after the first time. Choose it on purpose, so a second test of the same zone is not missed. Menus change; NinjaTrader’s current page wins.
The rule: every zone on your plan has its two alerts set before 9:25 a.m., sound on. Between alerts, the chart is not your job.
Getting it wrong is eyes on every candle from the open to the close, or a missed test because the alert was never set.
It reveals you do not trust your levels to be where the trade is, so you look for trades everywhere.
The fix is one line in the systems check on your pre-market sheet, the checklist finished before 9:25 a.m.: alerts, two per zone, set, sound on, and the number of zones.
A zone without both alerts is not on the plan.

segments.title: The plan only, and the close
sections: During The Session, The Plan Is The Only Input
The Close: Nothing New At 15:55, Platform Shut At 16:00

cues.text: During the session, the plan is the only input. It only tells you which part of the plan is in play.
A trade traces one chain: idea, setup, trigger, construction.

A branch, one if-then line written before the session. A level reached with its read, what price does there, on a closed bar. A trigger fired. A construction that fits. Nothing else asks for an order.
Price bounces hard at 12:15 off a spot on no plan. Not yours. One line in the notes, with the time. No order.
Price bounced. Price does that all day, for free.
An open trade ends at its target, its planned scale, the one partial exit set before entry, or its stop. Or by your hand, for four reasons.
One: the stop was hit.
Two: a Tier One release, a major scheduled release, five minutes away. You flatten at T minus five.
Three: the thesis, the if-then you wrote for the trade, broke on a candle close.
Four: the session is over.
A trade taking too long has none of those. That exit is tagged Too Early: out before any of the four.
The rule: no entry from a level not on the plan, and no manual exit outside the four reasons.
Getting it wrong is a midday entry from a price found on the screen. It reveals the screen became the plan when the plan went quiet.
The fix: a notes line beside the chart. Write what the session shows you, with the time. Writing is the action.
Now, the close. Your day ends at 4 p.m. Eastern, the Module 02 window. The futures keep trading. You do not.
At 3:55 p.m. an alarm sounds. Cancel any working entry order, one still waiting to fill, and take nothing new.
A trade still open keeps its bracket, the stop and target already working, until 4 p.m. Then flatten by hand: reason, session over.
Its execution mark, the Pass or Fail you give an exit afterwards, is Pass. Close the platform. Not minimised. Closed.
The rule: nothing new from 3:55 p.m.; flat and the platform closed at 4 p.m.
Getting it wrong is an entry at 3:58 because the level was right there. It reveals the screen decided when the day ended, not you.
The fix: two repeating alarms, 3:55 p.m., nothing new, and 4 p.m., flat, platform shut. An entry from 3:55 on is tagged Broke Rule, a broken hard rule.

cues.text: The end-of-day routine runs within an hour of the 4 p.m. close, every trading day, whatever the result.
It runs on a schedule, not on a result. A red day does not make it longer, and a green day does not skip it. Ten to twenty minutes.
Five steps, always in this order.
One: the chart mark-up.
Two: the post-exit fields and the execution mark.
Three: one line on the day.
Four: the screenshot or clip.
Five: the mental close.
The chart mark-up is a written pass over the day’s chart, level by level: reached or not, what price did there, and what you did.
Then, for each trade, write whether price reached your planned target after the exit. That is a research note. It never changes the execution mark. After the exit is not your money.
Step two. For every trade, complete the post-exit half of the journal from Module 18.
Exit price and reason, the R multiple, which is the result in units of your planned risk, time in trade, any tag, and the mark.
The execution mark is Pass or Fail, set after the exit. Did the exit follow the plan? Pass is one of six exits.
A target. The planned scale.
A pre-set invalidation, the price that says the idea was wrong. The stop.
Session end, or a flatten at T minus five.
Anything else is Fail.
The mark is kept apart from the grade, the A-plus to C you gave the setup at entry, so the grade never reads the outcome.
The outcome arrives after the exit and asks for a vote. It does not get one.
Step three is one line on the day, a sentence of fact: two trades, both from plan branches, one Fail, a manual exit on a stall. Not how the market behaved.
The rule: all five steps are finished within an hour of the close, every trading day, with every trade marked.
Getting it wrong is a routine that only runs after losing days, or marks filled in on Sunday from memory. It reveals the review has become a reaction to the result.
The fix: a repeating alarm inside the hour, labelled close routine, and five boxes in order. An empty mark the next morning is the first thing you fill in.

segments.title: Screenshots, the recording and the mental close

cues.text: The mark-up shows where price went. It cannot show what you saw when you acted, or how long you took. The screenshot and the recording can.
The screenshot: one per trade, entry and exit marked, saved with the trade.
In a line or two, write the level, the trigger, why the stop and target sat there, and the exit reason. Under a minute each.
The recording: record the whole session, then watch only the minutes around each trade, and around any alert you came to the screen for and did not trade.
Watch for what a chart cannot give back: when the information arrived, how long you took to act, and whether what you did matches what you wrote down.
The rule: one annotated screenshot per trade, every day, and the minutes around each trade watched.

Getting it wrong is a recording saved every day and never opened, or screenshots of winners only. It reveals the review picks what is comfortable to see. A folder of winners is a scrapbook, not a review.
The fix: name each clip with the date and entry time, and add a box for every trade: clip watched, yes or no. No tick, routine not finished.
Now, the mental close. The platform being shut does not mean the day is over.
It keeps running in your head: the exit you would take back, the move you missed at 2:10 p.m., the number on the account.
Carried into the evening, it becomes the next session’s first trade, taken to make up for the last one.
The mental close ends it: one written sentence that does not depend on your mood.
Day closed: two trades, one Pass, one Fail logged. Then the closing clause, in the page’s words: the next day starts from its own plan.
A count, a mark and an end. No promise to make anything back, and no grade by the result.
The rule: the routine ends with one sentence in the journal that starts Day closed, and after it, no charts until the pre-market routine.
Getting it wrong is reopening the chart at 8 p.m., or a sentence that ends with a promise to get it back. It reveals the next session is already being traded against this one.
The fix: a fixed template; anything outside it is crossed out. If the pull to look again is strong, one line in the notes, and leave it there.

cues.text: A hypothetical illustration, not a trade record: a composite session, invented prices, built to show the routine.
Four zones, two alerts each, set by 9:20 a.m.: the overnight high, the prior-day value high, the prior-day value low and the prior-day low.
Value high and value low edge the band where the prior session traded most. Two of the four carry branches.
Trade one, from the first branch. At 9:46 a.m. the near-edge alert sounds. Price accepts above the value high, closing and holding there, and the trigger fires on the pullback.
It ends at its stop. The mark is Pass: the stop is on the list. A planned trade that lost gets no negative tag. The post-loss reset from Module 02 runs.
At 10:24 a.m. price falls through the value low zone. Both alerts sound. No branch sits there, so nothing is taken. The alerts did their job. So did you, by doing nothing.
Trade two, from the failed-breakdown branch at the prior-day low: two closes below the zone, one back above, and the trigger fires from the reclaimed zone.
At 11:12 a.m. the trade has gone sideways for twenty minutes, and you close it by hand. None of the four reasons applies. Too Early, mark Fail.
At 12:15 p.m. a sharp bounce at a price on no plan. One line in the notes, no order.
At 3:55 p.m. the nothing-new alarm sounds; no orders working. At 3:57 a rearmed alert sounds at the value low zone: logged, nothing taken. At 4 p.m. you are flat, platform closed.
At 4:20 p.m. the routine runs. In the mark-up, trade two’s planned target was reached at 3:57, hours after the exit. A note. It changes neither mark.
Post-exit fields: trade one, Pass. Trade two, Too Early, Fail. One line on the day: two trades, both from plan branches, one Fail, a manual exit on a stall.
The clip around the manual exit shows the hand moving to the exit button after a stretch of looking at the account, not the chart.
The mental close at 4:41 p.m.: Day closed, two trades, one Pass, one Fail logged.
Notice what the routine did. The planned loss got no negative tag. The Fail was made visible, and no one had to feel bad. Where price went after the exit is a fact for your record.
The rule the session kept: no entry off the plan, nothing new after 3:55 p.m., every trade marked within the hour.

cues.text: Take your last five trading sessions. Score one point for each line that was true on all five.
One: alerts. Every zone on the plan had its two alerts set before 9:25 a.m.
Two: plan only. Every entry was from a level on that session’s plan.
Three: the close. No entry after 3:55 p.m., and the platform closed at 4 p.m.
Four: on schedule. The routine was finished within an hour of the close, on green and red days alike.
Five: every trade marked. Post-exit fields, execution mark, and a screenshot or clip, all done by the end of the routine.
Six: day closed. Each day ended with the one sentence, and no chart was reopened before the next pre-market routine.
The threshold. Six of six, keep going. Four or five: the missing lines are the first thing you set up before your next session.
Under four: the session is still running you. Start with line three and line five, because one ends the day and the other makes it a record.
A miss on line three counts as under four, whatever the total.
Getting it wrong is scoring a line true because it was true most days. A routine that runs on most days is a mood with a schedule.
The assignment. After your next close, write one sentence in your journal that starts Day closed.
Give the number of trades, how many were marked Pass, and the closing clause that the next day starts from its own plan. That is the whole assignment.
In one line: the plan decides the session, the clock ends it, and the routine records it.
Where it goes next. The post-exit fields and the Pass or Fail mark you fill in at the close are defined in Module 18, Journaling and Review.
Module 18 also covers the weekly review, held at a fixed time, where your Too Early count and your mark-up notes are read across the week.
The zones your alerts sit on come from Module 16, the pre-market routine, which finishes by 9:25 a.m. with the alerts set.
The window, the four flatten reasons and the kill switch that frame the session are in Module 02, the hard rules. Module 14 covers how the target and the one planned scale are set before entry.
The sources list the NinjaTrader help pages for alerts. Menus change, and the vendor’s current page wins.

check.q: How many sessions do you score?
check.why: A line scores a point only if it was true on all five.

check.q: You score 5 of 6, but you missed line three. That counts as…
check.why: A miss on line three counts as under four, whatever the total.

check.q: Where are the post-exit fields and the Pass or Fail mark defined?
check.why: Module 18, Journaling & Review, along with the weekly review.

check.q: Scoring a line true because it was true most days reveals…
options: A rule that is too strict
check.why: Most days is not all five.

questions.q: Which alerts does each zone on your plan carry?
options: One at the near edge and one at the far edge
One at the near edge only
One at the far edge only
questions.why: Two per zone: near edge and far edge, set before the session.

questions.q: At what time are you flat and the platform closed?
questions.why: Nothing new from 3:55 p.m.; flat and shut at 4 p.m. Eastern.

questions.q: A trade is taking too long and you close it by hand. That exit is…
questions.why: None of the four reasons applies, so it is tagged Too Early.

options: Set at entry from the grade
Pass or Fail, set after the exit by whether it followed the plan
questions.why: It is kept apart from the grade so the grade never reads the outcome.

questions.q: How long after the close does the routine run?
options: Only if the day was red
Within an hour, every trading day
questions.why: On a schedule, not on a result.

questions.q: How much of the recording do you watch?
options: The minutes around each trade, and any alert you came to the screen for
questions.why: Watch the minutes that matter, starting with a stop-out and a manual exit.

questions.q: The mental close sentence starts with…
questions.why: A count, a mark and an end.

questions.q: You score under 4 on the end-of-day test. Start with…
questions.why: Line three ends the day and line five makes it a record.
